articles.title: From slavery to today: The Black women who shaped America
articles.description: "If you don’t understand the history of Black women, you don’t understand the history of America." Those words from Nobel Prize-winning novelist Toni Morrison open Sasha Bonét's debut memoir, "The Waterbearers". The New York writer traces three generations of Black women in her family: her grandmother Betty Jean, the daughter of formerly enslaved people in Louisiana who went on to raise eleven children; her mother Connie, who sought a middle-class life in majority-white Houston; and Sasha herself, now raising her daughter Sofia in New York.

articles.description: Hurricane Polo is gaining strength as it moves along Mexico's southwestern coast as a Category 5 cyclone. The Miami-based National Hurricane Center reports Polo is an “extremely dangerous” storm with winds of 165 mph. It was centered Tuesday about 215 miles south of Zihuatanejo, Mexico, and stationary over the Pacific Ocean. Mexican authorities have suspended classes in several coastal areas as Polo brushed along the coastline. Heavy rain could cause flash flooding and mudslides in Guerrero and Michoacán states. articles.title: Republican Senate Nominee Who Backed Trump’s War Now Eating Her Words
articles.description: The Republican Senate nominee in Iowa is trying to criticize the Iran war’s effect on ordinary people—without mentioning President Trump or her own voting history. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran. We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices,” Representative Ashley Hinson posted on X Monday. Not surprisingly, Hinson’s solution doesn’t mention how Trump created the mess in the first place. Hinson also didn’t mention her own voting record: She has voted six times against House resolutions calling for Trump to end the war. Instead, she suggests “suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports, unleashing E-15 everywhere we can, reinstating the $1/gallon biodiesel tax credit, and creating a diesel relief program to help our farmers and truckers being crushed by the high costs.” “These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end,” Hinson said, adding that Iowa’s highway trust fund needed be “replenished, so that Iowans don’t suffer from crumbling roads and bridges while relief comes our way now.” Fuel prices have skyrocketed in the last seven months, thanks to Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz, and, more recently, the takeover of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea by Houthi forces in Yemen. The average price of gasoline as of Monday was $4.4786 nationally and $4.3698 in Iowa, according to the American Automobile Association . Diesel fuel prices are even worse: $6.5107 nationally and $6.3157 in Iowa, a state with a large agricultural economy whose equipment depends on diesel. Hinson is polling neck and neck with her Democratic opponent, state Representative Josh Turek, and is clearly worried that failing to acknowledge the war’s impact could hurt her in November. Trump won the state by 13 points in 2024, but Republicans and the president are polling lower and lower each day with the ongoing war only getting worse .

articles.title: Can cloud seeding fight drought? Startup Rainmaker just raised $100 million to find out
articles.description: Rainmaker, the weather modification startup focused on generating rain and snow through cloud seeding, announced today that it has raised $100 million in Series B funding. Investors including NOA VC, Upfront Ventures, DCVC, Lowercarbon Capital, and Dream Ventures participated in the round. Rainmaker declined to share an updated valuation as part of the news. Prior to this round, the company had raised $50.3 million in venture backing. Founded in 2023 (and dubbed “ the hardest startup in America ” by Fast Company ), Rainmaker has developed a fleet of custom drones that can withstand harsh conditions in order to “seed” precipitation. During flights, the drones release silver iodide, an ice-attracting particle, into clouds with promising conditions. The silver iodide serves as a catalyst, helping turn the cloud’s water droplets or ice crystals into precipitation. In recent months, the company says, it has made significant progress toward demonstrating the effectiveness of its seeding programs. Rainmaker says that it has data tying its flights to 145 million incremental gallons of freshwater: Its drones fly in programmed patterns, allowing researchers to distinguish their precipitation from naturally occurring precipitation. In August, test flights in Alaska’s Kenai Peninsula yielded 19 million gallons of precipitation over the course of three hours. Founder and CEO Augustus Doricko views the Alaska testing as a breakthrough moment. “That [research campaign] represents a significant, precedent-changing shift in our capacity to produce fresh water at scale for the ecosystems, communities, and industries that need it across the Colorado River Basin, the Great Salt Lake, the rest of the dry and arid western United States, and world over,” he says. The new funding will support the expansion of Rainmaker’s research team, including radar meteorologists, machine learning specialists, and aerosol chemists. Rainmaker also plans to continue collaborating with outside research teams in order to validate its results. Interest in weather modification is on the rise as climate change introduces new risks and concerns, from drought to increasingly powerful storms. Recast Systems, a newly-launched competitor, is seeding clouds with an organic compound in Texas and New Mexico. Doricko says that Rainmaker has filed patents for multiple biodegradable seeding agents and is preparing to test them this winter. If Rainmaker continues to make progress toward cloud seeding at scale, Doricko sees an opportunity to mitigate extreme weather, too. Hail storms, floods, tornadoes, hurricanes: it’s not hard to imagine that someone will be willing to pay to make events such as these less severe. “We will be better situated than anybody in history to conduct these subsequent interventions,” Doricko says. They fit within his broader vision to “make Earth more habitable.”
